title: The Crown on the Windowsill

topics.value_lesson: courtesy as play — bowing and waving to ordinary things (the cat, the lamp, the moon) makes the whole room feel seen and loved

spine: One small royal waits on a windowsill at bedtime for the moon to climb over the roof and light up her crown, then says good night to everything she loves before the crown goes down to rest.

crown_style.role: what the crown is made of — crayon-colored cardboard or a chain of daisies

segments.text: I remember a little princess named {princess_name}. She wore a blanket cape, much too big, and a crown of {crown_style}. Her bedroom was her palace. The lamp glowed like a throne-room fire. Grandmother stood guard by the door. "The moon will rise soon," she said. "Set your crown on the windowsill, and the moon might light it up." So the little princess hurried past the cardboard castle, where a paper knight stood on the wall. "Good night, Sir Knight!" she called. Then she climbed up by the window to wait. Waiting is hard for small royals.

"While we wait," said Grandmother, "shall we twirl the time away?" Yes! The little princess twirled. Her cape went whoosh. She twirled again, slow, slow, and her cape bloomed like a big bell. Then Grandmother asked, "What crown does a moon deserve to see? The cardboard crown, colored bright? Or the daisy crown, smelling sweet?" The little princess chose. She carried it carefully, carefully, past Sir Knight, and set it on the windowsill. "Now the moon can find it," she whispered. Waiting felt important now.

"While we wait," said Grandmother, "shall we say good evening to the whole court?" Yes! The little princess waved her slow royal wave, side to side, side to side, like a flag in a breeze. She waved to the royal cat on his cushion-throne, and gave him one soft pat. Then Grandmother asked, "What crown does a moon deserve to see? The cardboard crown, colored bright? Or the daisy crown, smelling sweet?" The little princess chose. She carried it carefully, carefully, and set it on the windowsill. "Now the moon can find it," she whispered.

Then a pale glow crept along the edge of the roof. Up climbed the moon, round as a coin. Its light found the crown on the glass, and tiny golden dots began to dance — across the ceiling, over the walls, onto the sleeping cat's back. "Why does the moon shine all by itself?" whispered the little princess. "My crown only shines when light finds it." Grandmother bowed from her post by the door. "Some things carry light," she said, "and some things share it. Both are grand." She smiled. "And how does a royal say good night to a moon?"

"A wave," said the little princess. "A slow, royal wave." She lifted her hand high and waved it side to side. Side to side. The moonlight twinkled on her crown, as if the moon were waving back. Then off came the crown. Clink. It was the loudest sound in the hushed room. Cape, crown, and slippers waited on the chair, glowing softly. One golden dot stayed above her pillow. Even grand princesses take off their crowns at night. And I remember, she slept like royalty.

"A bow," said the little princess. "A deep, deep bow." She bent down slowly, so slowly that her crown slid forward. She caught it with both hands. Grandmother bowed back from her post by the door. Then off came the crown. Clink. It was the loudest sound in the hushed room. Cape, crown, and slippers waited on the chair, glowing softly. One golden dot stayed above her pillow. Even grand princesses take off their crowns at night. And I remember, she slept like royalty.
